concepts.title: Electric Current, Potential Difference, and Ohm's Law
concepts.body: Electric current is defined as the net rate of flow of electric charges across any cross-section of a conductor (I = Q/t). Electric potential difference between two points is the work done to move a unit positive charge from one point to another (V = W/Q). Ohm's law states that at a constant temperature, the current flowing through a metallic wire is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends (V = I * R). A common misconception is that electric current gets used up or consumed as it passes through components in a series circuit; in reality, current remains constant throughout a single-loop series circuit because electric charge is conserved.

concepts.title: Resistance, Resistivity, and Combination of Resistors
concepts.body: Resistance (R) is the property of a conductor to oppose the flow of electric charges. It depends directly on the length of the conductor, inversely on its area of cross-section, on the nature of the material, and on temperature. Resistance does not depend on the magnitude of current or applied potential difference. Resistivity is an intrinsic property of a material representing its characteristic electrical resistance per unit dimensions. In a series combination, total resistance is the sum of individual resistances (R_eq = R1 + R2 + ...), which increases total circuit resistance. In a parallel combination, reciprocal of equivalent resistance is the sum of reciprocals of individual resistances (1/R_eq = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ...). Crucially, the equivalent resistance of a parallel circuit is always less than the smallest individual resistance. Parallel connections are used in household wiring so appliances can run independently at constant voltage.

concepts.title: Heating Effect of Electric Current and Electric Power
concepts.body: When current passes through a resistive wire, electrical energy dissipates as heat energy. Joule's law of heating specifies that heat generated is directly proportional to the square of current, resistance, and time duration (H = I^2 * R * t). This heating effect is applied in electrical appliances like irons, water heaters, and electric fuses, where excess current melts a fuse wire to protect circuits. Electric power (P) is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed (P = V * I = I^2 * R = V^2 / R). The commercial unit of electrical energy is kilowatt-hour (kWh), where 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 Joules.

formulas.title: Ohm's Law, Resistance, and Resistivity
formulas.body:
1. V = I * R [Volts (V)] where V = potential difference in volts (V), I = electric current in amperes (A), R = resistance in ohms (ohm).
2. R = rho * l / A [Ohms (ohm)] where R = resistance in ohms (ohm), rho = resistivity in ohm-meters (ohm m), l = length of conductor in meters (m), A = cross-sectional area in square meters (m^2).

formulas.title: Electric Power and Joule's Law of Heating
formulas.body:
1. H = I^2 * R * t [Joules (J)] where H = heat energy in joules (J), I = electric current in amperes (A), R = resistance in ohms (ohm), t = time in seconds (s).
2. P = V * I = I^2 * R = V^2 / R [Watts (W)] where P = electric power in watts (W), V = potential difference in volts (V), I = current in amperes (A), R = resistance in ohms (ohm).
Commercial Energy Unit Note: 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J.

examples.title: Calculations for Resistors in Mixed Combinations
examples.body:
Problem: Two resistors of 6 ohms and 12 ohms are connected (a) in series and (b) in parallel across a 6 V battery. Calculate the total resistance and circuit current for both cases.
Solution:
(a) Series combination:
Total resistance R_s = R1 + R2 = 6 + 12 = 18 ohms.
Current I_s = V / R_s = 6 / 18 = 0.33 A.
(b) Parallel combination:
1 / R_p = 1 / R1 + 1 / R2 = 1 / 6 + 1 / 12 = (2 + 1) / 12 = 3 / 12 = 1 / 4.
Total resistance R_p = 4 ohms.
Current I_p = V / R_p = 6 / 4 = 1.5 A.
Note that the equivalent parallel resistance (4 ohms) is smaller than the smallest individual resistor (6 ohms).

examples.title: Calculation of Heat Generated and Commercial Energy Consumption
examples.body:
Problem: An electric room heater rated 1000 W works for 2 hours daily. Find the heat produced in joules during this 2-hour duration and the electrical energy consumed in commercial units (kWh) over 30 days.
Solution:
Given: Power P = 1000 W, Time t = 2 hours = 2 * 3600 s = 7200 s.
Heat produced in 2 hours: H = P * t = 1000 W * 7200 s = 7,200,000 J = 7.2 x 10^6 J.
Daily energy consumed in kWh = Power in kW * Time in hours = (1000 / 1000) kW * 2 h = 1 kW * 2 h = 2 kWh.
Total commercial energy in 30 days = 2 kWh/day * 30 days = 60 kWh.

mcqs.question: Which of the following physical factors does NOT affect the electrical resistance of a metallic wire?
options: Area of cross-section of the conductor
mcqs.explanation: Resistance of a metallic conductor depends on its length, area of cross-section, material property (resistivity), and temperature. It is an inherent property of the conductor and does not depend on the current flowing through it.

mcqs.question: A metallic wire of resistance R is cut into 3 equal pieces. These three pieces are then connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance of the parallel combination?
mcqs.explanation:
Step 1: Resistance is directly proportional to length. When the wire is cut into 3 equal parts, the resistance of each part becomes r = R / 3.
Step 2: When these 3 pieces (each of resistance R / 3) are joined in parallel, the net resistance R_eq is given by 1 / R_eq = 1 / r + 1 / r + 1 / r = 3 / r = 3 / (R / 3) = 9 / R. Taking the reciprocal gives R_eq = R / 9.

mcqs.question: An electric bulb rated 220 V, 100 W is operated on a 110 V supply. What will be the power consumed by the bulb?
mcqs.explanation:
Step 1: Calculate the resistance of the bulb using R = V^2 / P. Using rated values: R = (220)^2 / 100 = 48400 / 100 = 484 ohms.
Step 2: Calculate new power consumed at V_new = 110 V using P_new = (V_new)^2 / R. P_new = (110)^2 / 484 = 12100 / 484 = 25 W.
